title: Freeze one array mask set; multibeam writes all periphery variants
idea: Ideal: masks cost nothing. Closest: freeze a single array reticle set for every product and density, and write the product-specific periphery and option layers with a massively parallel multi-e-beam direct-write tool, so new SKUs, CXL/PIM variants and bug fixes need zero new reticles.
why: Fact 4: leading-edge mask sets cost $20-40M and months; zero-NRE derivatives make niche and custom DRAM profitable and speed fixes.

title: Two-height nanoimprint template prints wordline trench and contact together
idea: Ideal: one stamp prints the whole cell. Closest: an e-beam master is replicated into two-height nanoimprint templates that imprint buried-wordline trenches and bitline-contact recesses in one resist step (dual-damascene in resist); array layers imprint only, periphery stays on DUV.
why: Fact 4: replaces 2-3 EUV exposures in the array with one NIL step at ~1/10 the tool capex, and the self-registered two-level pattern deletes one overlay budget; ~15-20% litho cost cut.

title: Nanosphere monolayer sets the capacitor lattice
idea: Reverse top-down patterning into bottom-up packing: spread a Langmuir-Blodgett monolayer of 40 nm silica spheres that close-pack into a hex lattice, shrink them by plasma, and use them as the etch mask for honeycomb capacitor holes.
why: Replaces the EUV/ArFi honeycomb capacitor-hole layer with a wet coating step; tool cost near zero.

title: Automotive-first entry: new U.S. fab bootstraps on 125 C premium
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: a new entrant builds a small 10-20k wafer/month fab tuned for the 125 C automotive and industrial grade that incumbents underserve, selling at 2-3x commodity prices to profit at low volume, then learns its way into commodity DRAM.
why: Capital intensity: lowers break-even scale and investor risk for a U.S. DRAM entrant; grows domestic know-how before the commodity fight.

title: One-mask cell array via self-aligned everything
idea: Minify array masks to one: a single DUV mandrel feeds self-aligned quadruple patterning in two orthogonal directions, and every later array layer (contacts, landing pads, capacitor holes) is defined by selective deposition and etch keyed to the prior topography, never by an overlay exposure.
why: Masks and EUV count: array EUV layers fall from 5-7 to 0 and array mask count drops roughly 80%, removing overlay error budgets and cutting litho share of wafer cost by about half.

title: 77-kelvin DRAM: crude poly-Si transistors hold charge for hours
idea: Box: MIM charge x solid-phase-crystallized poly-Si TFT (leaky at 300 K) x voltage sense amp x 2D x glass or Si x PECVD a-Si plus furnace crystallization. At 77 K off-current falls by >1e6, so grain-boundary-limited TFTs from a low-mask university flow meet retention for liquid-nitrogen-cooled racks.
why: Uses temperature to relax process quality (no single-crystal Si, no EUV-grade junctions) and nearly removes refresh; LN2 cooling overhead is a few W per W; risk is system-level cryo adoption.

title: Termite-mound fab: sealed mini-environments plus passive stack-effect ventilation
idea: Termite mounds hold a steady climate with chimneys and earth thermal mass; build the fab as sealed tool mini-environments in an ISO 8 hall, pre-condition makeup air through buried earth tubes and exhaust it through solar-heated chimneys, eliminating most ballroom fan-filter units.
why: Cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-25% of fab construction and ~40% of facility power; est. 30% less shell capex and 40% less HVAC energy.

title: Substitute leading-edge EUV nodes with relaxed-pitch DUV DRAM in idle fabs
idea: Re-tool existing U.S. 300 mm mature-logic fabs to make an ~18-20 nm DRAM entirely with ArF immersion SAQP using 2018-era cell layouts, sold as capacity memory where a cost-per-bit premium is tolerable. The shell, utilities and most tools already exist.
why: Capital and time: ~18-24 months and ~$2-4B versus $15B+ and 3-5 years, with zero EUV; cost per bit ~1.5-2x worse, but adds supply into a 4x-priced market.

title: Record-pressing father-mother-son electroforming multiplies nanoimprint stamps
idea: Borrowed from vinyl pressing, which electroforms a nickel 'father' from the lacquer master, then 'mothers', then hundreds of 'son' stampers: a 10-person shop takes one e-beam quartz master per DRAM array layer, electroforms nickel generations and casts UV-cured hybrid-polymer working stamps, selling cheap daughter templates to NIL fabs.
why: Fact 4: NIL cost is dominated by template price and wear; daughter replication can cut template cost per wafer 10-100x. Defect amplification across generations is the risk.

title: Sketch-grade DRAM standard turns yield fallout into supply
idea: Combine yield-fallout bins with workloads that natively tolerate 1% bit errors (Bloom filters, count-min sketches, embedding tables, quantized KV-cache). A JEDEC-style approximate grade with an SPD flag and OS allocator lets these dies ship rather than be scrapped, with public research clusters as anchor buyers.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer started ~5-10% immediately at zero capex (supply strategy, capital intensity).

title: Relax overlay budgets, ship imperfect arrays, remap at boot
idea: Inverts 'memory must leave the fab perfect'. Loosen the storage-node-to-landing-pad overlay spec ~2x so scanners use fewer alignment marks and rework drops; each 512-row subarray carries ~6% spare columns plus a tiny CAM that the controller fills at power-on from a self-test, remapping bad cells at 64-bit granularity like a flash translation layer.
why: Litho time and rework sit inside the ~55% depreciation share (fact 4); ~15-25% more wafers per scanner-hour for ~6% area overhead.

title: Dirty fab: class-1000 cleanroom plus massive remapping
idea: Minify cleanliness requirements 1000x and magnify redundancy: accept up to 30% bad bits per subarray and let a controller with an on-die defect map route around them like a Teramac crossbar.
why: Fab capital and yield: cleanroom spend and particle control capex fall sharply; dies that would be scrapped become sellable at derated capacity.

title: Backside periphery wiring frees the front for single-exposure DUV
idea: Rearrange wiring sides: move power rails and global sense-amp/decoder routing to backside metal after wafer thinning, which relaxes frontside metal pitch until single ArF immersion exposure works.
why: No EUV for periphery metal; ~3-5 fewer critical masks and lower IR drop.

title: Optical-disc mastering machines write imprint templates for old fabs
idea: Po: memory is mastered like Blu-ray discs. Repurpose idle optical-disc mastering machines (rotary phase-transition thermal lithography with sub-100 nm marks) to write large-area line/dot imprint templates, which feed nanoimprint tools placed in existing 2x-nm DRAM bays for array layers.
why: Template supply and EUV avoidance: template writing at ~1% of e-beam cost on idle equipment; NIL gives sub-20 nm periodic features in trailing fabs.

title: ABF-free ceramic package substrates sidestep the build-up film chokepoint
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: replace organic ABF build-up substrates (one dominant film supplier) with low-temperature co-fired glass-ceramic substrates and silver-sinter die attach, whose expansion matches silicon and which do not absorb moisture or creep at 125 C.
why: Scarce resource and U.S. manufacturability: LTCC lines are mature and domestic; removes an organic-substrate chokepoint and solder fatigue at high temperature.

title: LNG-style take-or-pay project finance for DRAM fabs
idea: Combine the LNG-terminal project-finance structure, where 20-year take-or-pay offtake contracts serve as collateral, with DRAM fabs. Hyperscalers pre-buy fixed-price bit capacity, federal loan guarantees cover construction, and the fab SPV borrows at infrastructure rates instead of memory-cycle equity.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4). Cutting WACC from ~12% to ~6% and stretching depreciation lowers wafer cost ~15-20% and de-risks U.S. builds.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordline: fully silicided polysilicon fill
idea: Constraint: zero tungsten. Fill the buried-wordline trench with doped polysilicon over the gate oxide, cap it with thin nickel or cobalt and anneal until the whole fill converts to NiSi/CoSi2 (full silicidation), then recess; no WF6 CVD and no TiN barrier.
why: Removes China-concentrated tungsten (~80%) and WF6 tools from the cell; fewer fill/CMP steps and the freed barrier volume lowers wordline resistance.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten from mine to monolayer
idea: Vertical integration across scales: Colorado molybdenite is refined domestically into MoO2Cl2/MoCl5 ALD precursors, and molybdenum replaces tungsten in buried wordlines and contacts, where its shorter electron mean free path gives lower resistance below 20 nm width.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint; ~20-30% lower wordline resistance permits longer wordlines and less periphery.

title: Controlled spalling from PV: peel device layers, reuse substrates tenfold
idea: Borrowed from IBM's solar controlled-spalling work, which peels 10-20 um silicon layers by plating a stressed nickel film and starting a crack: a small team spalls blank device layers off 300 mm substrates for epi or bonding, mounts them on cheap carriers and re-polishes the donor wafer for 5-10 reuses.
why: Scarce resource: cuts crystal growth, HPQ crucible and polysilicon demand per bit 5-10x and yields thin dies for stacking; surface roughness and crack control are risks.

title: Hermit-crab strategy: retrofit idle LCD panel fabs for oxide-TFT memory
idea: Hermit crabs move into empty shells; buy idle Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED backplane fabs (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, IGZO TFT lines installed) and run 2T0C gain-cell arrays at 1-2 um rules on glass (~30 GB per panel) for capacity-tier CXL memory, bonded to small CMOS controllers.
why: Panel-fab capex per square meter is ~1/30 of a DRAM fab and exists idle now, so capacity memory arrives in months rather than 3-5 years (fact 4); US-sited panel lines add domestic supply.

title: Rubber-stamp inhibitor printing: the one added master is a stamp
idea: Use a hard-PDMS stamp as the only added pattern master to microcontact-print an ALD inhibitor monolayer in the BEOL, then grow the oxide-semiconductor channel and gate dielectric by area-selective ALD only on unstamped areas, so the memory layer needs no resist, exposure or etch.
why: Capital/steps: replaces ~6 litho/etch/strip steps and scanner time with one stamp contact; a stamp costs ~1% of a mask set.

title: Half-billion-dollar DRAM line from scavenged 200 mm tools
idea: Inverts 'a memory fab costs $15B'. A consortium buys decommissioned steppers, LPCVD furnaces, RIE and CMP tools at ~3-10% of new price, refurbishes them for a single tier-stacked DRAM flow needing only >=180 nm litho, and replicates the line as identical $0.5B modules.
why: Capital per wafer start ~20-30x lower; profitable even at lower density when tier count supplies the bits (fact 4).

title: MAPPER revived for arrays: all beamlets write one shared tile
idea: MAPPER's 13,000-beam maskless e-beam went bankrupt in 2018 because its data path (petabits per wafer) and throughput never closed. Memory arrays repeat one cell billions of times, so drive every beamlet from one shared on-chip blanking pattern broadcast to all, collapsing the data path ~1e6x, and use it only for the 3-5 array layers while periphery stays on DUV.
why: EUV dependence and mask cost: replaces EUV scanners and masks on array layers with a ~$30M maskless tool; saves ~$10M+ mask sets per node and removes the single-supplier EUV chokepoint for those layers.

title: Doping-superlattice 3D DRAM: porosify p+ layers instead of SiGe
idea: Constraint: no SiGe epitaxy, because strain caps the tier count. Grow fast all-silicon epi with alternating p+/p- doping, then electrochemically porosify only the p+ layers from the vertical-bitline slit to open lateral cavities for capacitors and gates, allowing 100+ tiers without strain relaxation.
why: Fact 2: clears the ~26-tier break-even with high-rate Si epi (~3x throughput vs Si/SiGe) and no misfit dislocations; cost per tier falls.

title: Xe: 172 nm excimer photons clean wafers inside load-locks
idea: Mount Xe2* excimer VUV lamps inside tool load-locks so every wafer gets a ~30 s photolysis in N2 that breaks organic and airborne molecular contamination before each deposition, replacing routine wet pre-cleans between steps.
why: Water: removes dozens of inter-step wet cleans with zero added queue time; those steps' water falls ~100%.

title: 2050 engineer's bottom-up fab: area-selective deposition replaces cut masks
idea: From 2050, deposit-everywhere-then-etch looks wasteful. Use area-selective ALD with inhibitor monolayers (aminosilane SAMs or small-molecule inhibitors that block dielectric so films grow only on metal) to grow landing pads, caps and self-aligned vias only where the layer below already defines them, deleting separate cut/block masks and their overlay budget.
why: Removes ~6-10 of ~60 mask steps and their overlay error, giving lower litho capex and ~10% fewer process days. Risk: selectivity is lost beyond ~5-10 nm of growth, so periodic etch-back cycles are needed.

title: PCB laser direct imaging: maskless DUV for low-volume periphery layers
idea: PCB makers dropped phototools for DMD laser direct imaging; apply a 193/248 nm micromirror-array maskless writer to DRAM's relaxed periphery layers (40 nm and up) and HBM base-die redistribution layers, so custom memory variants need no new reticle set.
why: Mask capital and agility: a DRAM mask set costs $10-30M+; custom low-volume AI memory becomes nearly mask-free; the throughput penalty is tolerable on a few layers.

title: Eliminate periphery photomasks: maskless micromirror digital lithography for relaxed layers
idea: Expose the 20-30 relaxed periphery and implant-class layers with a digital-micromirror maskless writer (as used in advanced packaging) pushed to 248/193 nm, so no reticles are bought, stored or requalified per product.
why: Capital and agility: removes ~$3-8M of masks per product revision and cuts new-variant ramp time from months to days.

title: Al: aluminum-infiltrated block copolymers pattern capacitor holes dry
idea: Thermally anneal a block copolymer into a hexagonal hole lattice matched to cell pitch, infiltrate one block with trimethylaluminum/ozone vapor pulses to make AlOx, then O2-plasma away the polymer to leave a dry hardmask.
why: Water and litho: replaces the EUV hole layer and its wet track with self-assembly plus vapor infiltration that uses negligible water (>10x cut for that layer).

title: Vertical plated-wire memory: NiFe-lined holes through word-plane stack
idea: Revive 1960s plated-wire memory (NiFe electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, non-destructive readout, flown in Apollo-era and Skylab systems): etch vertical holes through an epitaxial stack of heavily doped silicon word planes by metal-assisted chemical etching, electroplate a circumferentially magnetized NiFe film on each hole wall around a copper core, and store a bit where each word plane crosses a hole. A word current tilts the magnetization slightly and the core senses the induced voltage without destroying it.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a 3D array from one critical hole mask using only aqueous etch and plating (no rare gas), with readout that avoids destructive read and writeback. Risks are mV-level read signal below 100 nm and word-plane selectivity.

title: Waterless fab: supercritical CO2 replaces ultrapure water rinse
idea: Reverse wet to dry: replace most UPW rinse and post-etch clean steps with supercritical CO2 plus co-solvent cleaning in closed recycle loops; this also prevents capillary collapse of high-AR capacitor pillars.
why: Water and energy intensity drop ~50-70%, the pillar-collapse yield loss that limits AR goes away, and fabs can sit at water-stressed U.S. sites.

title: Optical-disc molding lines make spiral-crossbar memory discs
idea: The optical-disc industry collapsed under streaming, idling injection-molding lines that replicate ~100 nm grooves into a disc every ~3 seconds for cents. Mold one disc with clockwise and one with counter-clockwise sub-one-turn spiral grooves, metallize and polish them, and laminate the discs around a threshold-switching memory film so each pair of spirals crosses exactly once, with both line families reaching a CMOS hub chip bonded at the center.
why: Meets 100x: ~200,000 lines per family gives ~4e10 cells per disc pair for well under $1 of patterning, est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB with 2 bits/cell. Trades: density falls with radius, odd geometry, slow switching film.

title: Case hardening: fully silicided poly buried wordlines without tungsten
idea: Steel case hardening converts a surface in place by diffusion rather than depositing a coating; fill buried-wordline trenches void-free with doped poly-Si, then convert the upper part fully to NiSi or C54 TiSi2 by metal deposition and anneal, keeping a thin poly region near the drain for low GIDL.
why: W-free (constraint) with fewer steps (fact 4): poly fills sub-10 nm trenches without seams, needs no WF6 or nucleation barrier, and silicide reaches ~15 uOhm-cm, competitive with scaled W.

title: Bit-significance-aware arrays: dense sloppy LSB mats, robust MSB mats
idea: Combine the numeric structure of AI tensors with DRAM layout. One mask set prints two mat types: LSB mats at a near-failure tight pitch running ~1% BER, and sign/exponent/MSB mats at relaxed pitch. The controller swizzles each word so low-significance mantissa bits land in the dense mats.
why: About half the bits in BF16/FP8 tensors are low mantissa bits, so putting them in ~25% denser mats gives ~10-15% more bits per wafer with no new node (density, cost/bit).

title: Convert idle 3D NAND toolsets into vertical-bitline 3D DRAM lines
idea: Combine the 3D NAND toolset (staircase, channel-hole etch, replacement gate) with a vertical-bitline, horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM whose steps map one-to-one onto NAND tools: the alternating stack becomes Si/SiGe or oxide-semiconductor layers, the channel hole becomes the bitline hole, and gate replacement becomes capacitor replacement.
why: Reuses existing $10-20B NAND fabs instead of 3-5-year, $15B+ greenfield DRAM fabs. NAND tools already handle 200+ layers, far past the ~26-tier break-even (facts 2, 4).

title: Meet-in-the-middle capacitor: etch half from front, half from back
idea: Reverse the etch direction for half the hole: etch the storage-node hole to ~35:1 from the front, then after bonding to a carrier and thinning, etch the second 35:1 half from the backside and land it on an etch-stop plug at mid-depth; the two halves join into one 70:1+ electrode.
why: Capacitor charge wall and high-AR etch tool cost: doubles effective AR (to ~130:1 equivalent) using two easier etches, ~1.6-2x Cs or a relaxed mold etch with fewer cryo-etch chambers.

title: Audio-RAM trick revived: sell fail-bin DRAM behind remapping controllers
idea: In the 1980s, partially defective DRAMs were sold cheaply as 'audio RAM' until digital systems demanded perfect parts. Revive it for computing: fail-bin dies (bad rows, weak-retention cells, HBM stacks with one dead die) ship with a full fault map in SPD flash, a CXL controller remaps bad rows per page, and retention-weak parts run chilled to 0 C or at 32 ms refresh.
why: Meets 100x for its slice: dies otherwise scrapped (~10-20% of DRAM output, 20-30% of HBM) sell near scrap value, ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: supply limited to a few % of bits, controller complexity, slightly higher refresh power.

title: Cell biologist's membranes: block-copolymer self-assembly below 250 C
idea: Cell membranes self-organize into 4 nm bilayers with no instructions. Coat a high-chi silicon-containing block copolymer (e.g., PS-b-PDMS) into coarse DUV guide trenches; a 200-250 C thermal or solvent-vapor anneal self-assembles 8-10 nm half-pitch hole and line arrays, which transfer as hard masks for array layers.
why: Replaces 2-3 EUV or quad-patterning passes with a ~$2M coater and hotplate, all inside 400 C. Risks: defect density (target <0.01/cm2) and placement error.

title: Slip-form pour: grow capacitor pillars upward by dual selective deposition
idea: Like slip-forming a concrete silo that climbs as it pours, grow the storage-node pillar and its mold together from the landing-pad pattern: alternate area-selective ALD of TiN-on-TiN and SiO2-on-SiO2 with inhibitors swapped each supercycle, plus periodic etch-back defect correction, so no deep hole is ever etched.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the 60-75:1 etch (the costliest etch fleet), with no bowing or twisting, allowing AR>100 and ~2x Cs.

title: Substitute interposer wiring with glass-core millimetre unterminated memory links
idea: Place LPDDR-class dies within 1 mm of the processor on a glass-core panel substrate with 2 um lines, and replace terminated DDR signaling with unterminated 0.2 V-swing CMOS links that behave like on-die wires; panel glass replaces silicon interposers.
why: Constraint: I/O energy falls from ~5-10 to ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit (>=10x on the I/O share); capital: 510x515 mm glass panels cost a fraction of silicon interposers and need no TSVs.

title: Single ink whose function is set by laser dose
idea: Minify materials from six inks to one: print one In-Zn oxide precursor everywhere, then a laser dose map sets each region as conductor, semiconductor or insulator by controlling oxygen-vacancy density.
why: Process steps and tool count: one print station plus one digital laser replaces multiple deposition-litho-etch loops.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers woven into memory fabric
idea: Worse: build memory only by stacking films on flat plates. Flip: draw a macroscopic metal/semiconductor/insulator preform into kilometers of fiber whose cross-section holds a storage capacitor and an access junction. Weave orthogonal fibers into a crossbar fabric so every crossing is an addressable cell.
why: Capital: fiber towers cost ~$1M and run km/hour with no lithography, a speculative path to cheap bulk capacity.

title: Inductive coupling replaces TSVs in stacked DRAM
idea: Minify die-to-die vias to zero: thin each die to 10 um and pass data through on-chip inductor coils stacked over each other, with power delivered through a single edge-plated rail, removing TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes the TSV process module and its 20-30% yield loss, recovering area spent on TSV keep-out zones.

title: Federal offtake guarantees for old-tool tier-stacked DRAM
idea: Inverts 'markets fund only leading-edge memory'. DoD/DOE sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts at a fixed $/GB for DRAM-class memory made on >=180 nm tool lines in the U.S., with the price ratcheting down as tier counts rise.
why: De-risks capital for old-tool high-tier flows and secures defense/critical-infrastructure supply.

title: Liberty-ship fab modules: identical U.S. fabs built serially
idea: Time-compress fab construction from 3-5 years to ~15 months by freezing one standard 20k-wafer-per-month module (shell, utilities, layout) and building copies serially from prefabricated U.S.-made subfab skids, as WWII yards cut ship build time 10x through repetition.
why: Learning-curve cost ~20-30% lower by the fifth copy; earlier revenue cuts interest during construction (capital intensity).

title: Inspection-free fab using on-die sensors and boot-time self-repair
idea: Po: the fab never looks at its wafers. Remove most inline defect inspection and CD metrology; embed ring oscillators, capacitor-leak monitors and array test structures in every die that report process health at sort, and raise defect tolerance with 2x spare rows/columns plus boot-time soft remapping.
why: Capital intensity: inspection/metrology ~10-15% of tool capex plus cycle time; trades ~2% die area for ~10% lower capex and faster cycles.

title: High-chi block copolymer multiplies DUV hole density fourfold
idea: Magnify density without new optics: coarse DUV guide posts direct a high-chi block copolymer to self-assemble 4 cylinders per guide at ~12 nm, used for landing pads and storage-node contacts.
why: Lithography: removes 1-2 EUV layers per die; DSA tooling is a track, not a scanner.

title: Eliminate burn-in ovens: on-die heaters stress dies during wafer sort
idea: Add a thin metal heater mesh under each die and use internal charge pumps to apply elevated VPP/VARY while heating dies to ~125 C at the prober, screening infant mortality without package burn-in ovens. Shipped parts are standard DDR5/HBM3E; the heaters are left floating.
why: Removes burn-in boards, ovens and hours of cycle time, and screens before packaging so bad dies never consume HBM stacking cost.

title: Backside-etched trench capacitors use the wafer itself as mold
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: after front-end transistors are bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer to ~3 um and etch capacitor trenches from the back into the silicon under each access transistor, using crystalline silicon as the mold (no carbon mold, no support mesh) for ~25 fF cells.
why: Facts 1 and 3: 4-5x Cs buys 125 C retention; front-side contact AR collapses and the capacitor mold and support-lattice deposition steps disappear.

title: Substitute copper die-to-die wires with microLED free-space optical links
idea: Each DRAM die face carries arrays of mass-transferred GaN micro-LEDs and silicon photodiodes (1-2 Gb/s per lane, thousands of lanes) that talk across the stack or to the processor through short imaging optics, replacing TSV/microbump buses and SerDes.
why: Constraint: ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit versus 3-15 pJ/bit (>=10x); facet: no TSV etch/fill and no microbump yield loss (fact 6), using display-industry microLED transfer.

title: A million zone plates steered by Texas micromirrors write maskless
idea: Zone-plate array lithography: a plate of ~10^6 diffractive micro-lenses, each switched by a U.S.-made DLP micromirror, focuses its own spot so the whole field is written in parallel without a mask or projection lens.
why: Maskless domestic patterning at ~30-40 nm with a ~$10M tool; pitch splitting finishes the array.

title: Al: self-ordered anodic alumina pores replace EUV capacitor-hole patterning
idea: Deposit Al over the storage-node landing pads, pre-texture with a coarse DUV guide pattern, then anodize so pores self-organize at a voltage-set pitch (~2.5 nm/V) and grow straight to AR >100:1 with no plasma etch; line the pores with TiN/ZrO2/TiN to form the capacitors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the EUV hole layer and the slowest high-AR dry etch while reaching AR beyond 115 for more Cs; ~30-40% capacitor-module cost cut claimed.

title: Brewed S-layer protein crystals as sub-EUV lithography templates
idea: Ferment bacteria whose surface-layer proteins self-assemble into 2D crystals with hexagonal ~10-15 nm lattices, recrystallize them on wafers over a coarse DUV guide pattern, and use the pores as metal-deposition or etch templates for landing pads and capacitor seeds.
why: Fact 4: lattice period is genetically fixed below EUV pitch and costs grams from a fermenter, replacing an EUV exposure per layer.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing makes mask-free personalization layers on glass
idea: Worse: buy a new mask set for every memory variant. Flip: on standard glass-panel memory arrays, write the variable layers (wordline strapping, redundancy routing, I/O fan-out) with multi-nozzle e-jet printing of nanoparticle inks at ~100 nm, so one array panel serves many products.
why: Masks/capital: zero mask cost per variant makes low-volume specialty memory viable.

title: Eliminate multi-year construction: factory-built containerized fab modules
idea: Build standardized 2,500 wafer-per-month array-line modules, with tools pre-installed in sealed clean containers with integrated utilities, in a shipyard-style factory, and bolt them onto an on-site utility spine one module at a time.
why: Capital and time: fab-to-first-wafer from 3-5 years to ~12-18 months, and capacity added in $1-2B steps instead of $15B, matching scarcity-driven demand.

title: Eliminate access-transistor lithography: grow vertical nanowire channels from catalysts
idea: Place catalyst dots with a block-copolymer lattice (no mask), grow vertical single-crystal Si nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid epitaxy with a CMOS-friendly catalyst (Al or Cu-silicide), then wrap them in ALD gate stacks to form 4F2 vertical access transistors.
why: Facts 2 and 4: removes the EUV-class active-area and channel etch masks; bottom-up wires have smooth sidewalls and low trap density, tightening the leakage tail.

title: Hot-wire sweep zone-anneals block copolymers into defect-free arrays
idea: Effect: directional ordering in a moving thermal gradient (zone annealing). A heated wire or line-focused IR lamp crosses a BCP film at um/s, and domains order like a directional solidification front that pushes defects to the edge, reaching long-range order in minutes instead of hours in an oven. A $40k sweeper plus ~$600k of university fab time tests 14 nm half-pitch bitline gratings.
why: Fact 4: defectivity kept DSA out of DRAM; below 0.01 defects/cm2, DSA could replace SAQP passes at ~1/5 the cost.

title: Four bonded DUV array tiers beat one EUV tier on density
idea: First principle: cost per bit = wafer cost / bits. A fully depreciated, DUV-only 16 nm-class 6F2 array wafer gives ~56% of the bits of a 12 nm EUV wafer at roughly half its cost, and face-to-back hybrid bonding of four such array tiers onto one periphery wafer, linked by ~1 um inter-tier vias, gives ~2.2x bits per footprint.
why: EUV dependence and capital (fact 4): cost per bit at parity to ~10% lower with zero EUV, about 2x density per package footprint, all on installed tools.

title: Rutile TiO2 on RuO2 doubles k and halves capacitor etch
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: grow Al-doped rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100), templated below 400 C by RuO2 electrodes whose high work function plus Al doping suppress hot Schottky leakage, so capacitor aspect ratio drops from ~70 to ~35.
why: Facts 1 and 4: single-step capacitor etch, thinner carbon hardmask, fewer support layers; capacitor module cost ~-30%.

title: Nanoporous-gold dealloying grows a sponge-surface storage electrode
idea: Borrowed from catalyst and supercapacitor makers, who leach the less-noble metal out of an alloy to get 10-50x surface area: deposit a Ru-Al alloy bottom electrode, dealloy the Al in mild base to leave porous Ru with 3-5 nm ligaments, then conformally coat dielectric and top electrode.
why: Fact 1: 2-3x effective electrode area gives AR-115-class charge at AR ~60; a metallic, low-resistance descendant of 1990s HSG silicon. Pore clogging inside a 20 nm node is high risk.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrodes multiply capacitor area inside shallow holes
idea: Effect: dealloying (selective dissolution plus surface-diffusion coarsening). Deposit a Ru-Al or Ti-Al alloy liner in a low-AR (~15:1) hole and dissolve the Al to leave a bicontinuous porous electrode with 10-20 nm ligaments; then ALD a thin high-k and a top TiN. Surface area per footprint rises 4-6x.
why: Fact 1: reaching 5 fF without AR 60-75 removes HAR mold etch and pattern-collapse controls, which are among the costliest capacitor-module tools.

title: Frozen-node DRAM: depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: Minify node changes to zero: design a DRAM generation that never shrinks and is upgraded only by stacking more dies per package, so tools run 15 years instead of a 5-year depreciation schedule.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; tripling tool life cuts wafer cost roughly 30-35%, while a node only buys 10-20%.

title: Open-standard modular fab tools with swappable chambers
idea: First principle: a process tool is a vacuum chamber plus a few energy and gas sources, and most of its price is integration, not physics. Define an open mechanical, electrical and software chamber standard so U.S. vendors build interchangeable process modules that are repaired, upgraded and redeployed on common transfer platforms over 25-year lives.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: lower tool cost, longer asset life, less vendor lock-in.

title: Eliminate spare rows, columns and fuses: DDR5 on-die ECC absorbs defects
idea: Remove most row/column redundancy and fuse banks; single-cell hard faults stay in place for the existing DDR5 on-die SEC ECC and Error-Check-and-Scrub to correct, with a small spare pool kept only for cluster faults. The DDR5 interface and its ECS reporting are unchanged.
why: Frees ~3-5% of die area and removes fuse-programming test time, a few percent more bits per wafer at no tool cost.

title: Resurrected-scanner fab: build on the industry's retired DUV tools
idea: Reverse the tool lifecycle: buy retired KrF/ArF dry scanners and older etchers on the secondary market, refurbish them, and pair them with a design rule set made only for spacer multiplication and self-alignment.
why: Litho capex falls ~90% compared with a new EUV fab and tools ship in months, not years; this suits a U.S. startup fab.

title: Substrate-agnostic memory qualification standard unlocks non-silicon suppliers
idea: Worse: write qualification specs that implicitly assume bulk-Si dies and block every alternative. Flip: create a JEDEC/OCP 'memory tile' standard defined only by electrical, thermal and reliability behavior plus a tile form factor, with funded shared qualification labs, so glass, SiC or ceramic memory is qualified once and bought widely.
why: Strategy: removes the ~2-3-year qualification barrier for non-Si capacity and attracts new capital.

title: Mandated U.S. second-source licensing of DRAM designs, 1970s-style
idea: Revive the 1970s-80s rule, enforced by military and big buyers, that every memory part had a licensed second source (the Intel 1103 was second-sourced): require that DRAM bought in volume by federal agencies and subsidized hyperscalers has a licensed U.S. second source, with design, test programs and process recipes transferred under royalty.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: transfers proven designs instead of each new entrant spending 5+ years of learning; could seed ~5-10% domestic supply on existing logic or legacy lines within ~3 years.

title: Atmospheric spatial-ALD tools for capacitor high-k without vacuum chambers
idea: Box: ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x 300 mm Si x spatial ALD. Wafers rotate under gas-bearing heads with separated precursor and oxidant zones at atmospheric pressure, so growth rate is decoupled from purge time; pressure-pulsed dwell zones let precursor diffuse to the bottom of 70:1 holes before the wafer moves on.
why: Throughput and tool capex for the capacitor module: 5-10x wafers/hour per tool vs temporal ALD and no vacuum hardware, saving hundreds of millions per 100k-wafer fab; risk is step coverage at AR 70.

title: Substitute quartz crucibles with electromagnetic cold-crucible silicon crystal growth
idea: Melt silicon in a water-cooled segmented copper crucible where induction currents push the melt off the walls (skull melting), and pull single crystals from the levitated pool under a cusp magnetic field. No fused-quartz crucible is consumed and oxygen from SiO2 dissolution disappears.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz chokepoint (>80%); oxygen-free crystals avoid oxygen precipitates that feed junction-leakage tails (fact 3).

title: Directed self-assembly confined to DRAM's honeycomb capacitor array
idea: Directed self-assembly was abandoned for logic because defect density stalled and logic layouts are not periodic. DRAM's storage-node array is a hexagonal lattice, the native pattern of cylinder-forming block copolymers, so DUV-printed guide trenches (graphoepitaxy) multiply hole density 4-7x and residual defects are absorbed by existing row/column redundancy.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV exposures with a ~$1M coat/anneal track; cost per patterned layer down ~5x; defect spec relaxed from logic-grade to repairable-grade.

title: One ALD chemistry family builds every layer of the cell
idea: First principle: tool count scales with the number of distinct materials in the flow. Make the channel (IGZO), electrodes (degenerate In2O3:H/ITO), dielectric (Ga2O3/HfO2 laminate) and passivation from one In/Ga/Zn/Hf precursor set in one multi-station ALD cluster, changing only cycle ratios and oxidant.
why: Capital and tool set: ~5 tool types collapse into one platform, with a simpler U.S. tool supply chain.

title: Food-packaging spatial ALD: conveyor-speed liners and spacers
idea: Roll-to-roll barrier-film lines for food packaging coat by moving the substrate under fixed precursor and purge zones; use atmospheric spatial ALD heads for DRAM's low-aspect-ratio ALD films (spacers, liners, periphery gate stacks) and reserve slow temporal ALD only for the deep capacitor stack.
why: Tool capex (fact 4): spatial ALD runs 5-10x more wafers/hour on thin conformal films; claim ~30% fewer ALD chambers per fab.

title: Atmospheric spatial-ALD zinc-tin-oxide cells for 200C downhole tools
idea: Extreme user: 200C oil and geothermal downhole tools needing indium-free, wide-bandgap channels. Deposit the ZnSnO channel and Al2O3/HfO2 gate stack with gas-bearing atmospheric spatial-ALD heads (no vacuum chamber, ~100+ wafers/h), giving a vacuum-free BEOL gain-cell module that stacks over any logic wafer.
why: Capital/scarce resource: spatial-ALD heads cost ~1/4 of vacuum ALD/sputter clusters, no indium, and any depreciated logic fab can add memory tiers.

title: Mitotic-spindle field assembly places pre-grown nanowire access transistors
idea: The spindle lines chromosomes up at the metaphase plate with fibers and forces; grow single-crystal Si or oxide-semiconductor nanowire transistors in bulk off-wafer, suspend them in a dielectric fluid and use AC electrode arrays to pull one into each cell site by dielectrophoresis, then bond and contact them.
why: Takes transistor making off the array wafer, removing ~10 front-end masks and high-temperature steps and letting arrays be built on cheap substrates; est. 30% fewer wafer process steps.

title: Commodity trader's forward curve: hyperscaler-funded DRAM capacity options
idea: Grain markets finance planting with forward contracts. Hyperscalers buy tradable 10-year wafer-start options on a new fab, prepaying 30-40% of capex at a strike price and keeping the right to resell on an exchange; builders get capital at near-sovereign cost while demand risk shifts to buyers who can hedge it.
why: Cuts the cost of capital, and the boom-bust risk premium in DRAM pricing, by maybe 3-5 points, making $15B fabs financeable sooner and damping 4x price swings. Risks: contract enforcement and antitrust.

title: Resonant-tunneling InAs/AlSb floating gate from compound-semiconductor fabs
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: a triple-barrier InAs/AlSb heterostructure is opaque at rest (AlSb ~2.1 eV conduction offset) but turns transparent when ~2.5 V aligns its resonant level, letting electrons enter or leave an InAs floating gate fast and at low energy while retention is non-volatile (ULTRARAM-type), grown on Si by MBE/MOCVD.
why: Zero refresh; switching energy per area ~100x below flash and demonstrated endurance >1e7; uses U.S. III-V epitaxy capacity instead of DRAM fabs and needs no HAR capacitor; the endurance gap is covered by write buffering (facts 3, 4).

title: Shape after printing: angled ion beam stretches DUV features
idea: Rearrange litho into litho-plus-sculpt: print one relaxed ArF layer, then use angled reactive ion beams to elongate or merge holes and slots in one direction, replacing the second exposure of double patterning.
why: Halves the number of critical DUV exposures without EUV and cuts process steps per layer ~30%.

title: One universal grating reticle prints every array layer
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own critical mask'. Lay out all array layers (active, wordline, bitline, storage node) on a single gridded honeycomb lattice so one ultra-high-quality periodic reticle prints the dense lines for every layer by rotation/offset, and only coarse DUV-printable cut/keep masks are layer-specific.
why: ~60-70% fewer critical reticles and qualification cycles, and a path to replace 3-4 EUV layers with DUV cut layers (fact 4).

title: Cr: chrome-free interference lithography prints periodic cell arrays
idea: Because cell arrays are perfectly periodic, expose them with multi-beam 193 nm immersion interference (no photomask, no chrome absorber) to produce line and hole lattices, using one cheap trim mask for array edges.
why: Interference tools cost ~1/10 of a scanner and need no mask; with one spacer doubling they reach ~20 nm half-pitch for the array.

title: Five-mask array wafer: sense amps live on bonded logic wafer
idea: Constraint: the array wafer gets five masks (active, wordline, bitline, capacitor, bond pad). Sense amplifiers, decoders and all upper metal sit on a separately made CMOS wafer hybrid-bonded face-to-face, with a 16:1 local bitline-select device formed in the same wordline step so bond pitch can stay near 0.5 um.
why: Fact 7: the ~49% periphery moves to a cheap logic node and stops occupying DRAM-process area; array wafer cost -50%, array die density ~1.8x.

title: Refurbished dry-ArF and KrF fleets run wider-tolerance array layers
idea: Combine the abundant used-tool market (refurbished dry ArF, KrF and older etchers) with cell-level error tolerance. Non-critical and semi-critical layers go to tools with ~2x worse CD uniformity and chamber matching, and the added variability (~0.1-0.5% bit errors) fits the 1% budget.
why: Used tools cost 10-30% of new, so a greenfield U.S. fab could cut capex ~20% and ramp sooner by sourcing tools immediately (capital, time, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Single-crystal tiers by repeated low-temperature layer transfer
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: polysilicon tiers leak too much hot, so each 3D tier is a 50 nm crystalline Si film split from a donor by hydrogen implant and bonded below 400 C, with laser dopant activation; the donor is reused, and each tier costs one bond plus ~3 masks.
why: Fact 2: crystalline channels keep the 125 C leakage tail of planar DRAM while stacking; no epi superlattice and no single 100:1 etch.

title: Substitute sense amplifiers with complementary n-IGZO/p-SnO oxide gain cells
idea: Pair n-type IGZO and p-type SnO (or Cu2O) thin-film transistors in a 3T cell whose storage node gates a CMOS-like inverter, so a read drives a rail-to-rail level onto a short local line with no sense amplifier and no restore. Sputtered below 350 C, patterned with ArF only, stackable in BEOL.
why: Constraint: no precharge/restore and bit-granular reads remove the 128x overfetch, ~0.1-0.3 pJ per useful bit versus 5.9 pJ (>=20x); facet: DUV-only BEOL stack runnable in logic or display fabs. Poor p-oxide mobility is the risk.

title: Three-beam interference lithography for all dense hexagonal array layers
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: one maskless tool interfering three 193 nm beams at 120 degrees prints the honeycomb lattice for active islands, capacitor holes and landing pads by only changing phase and rotation; spacer doubling brings it to ~40 nm hex pitch and a cheap DUV block mask trims the array edges.
why: No reticle and simple optics: tool cost perhaps 1/20 of EUV and 1/5 of an immersion scanner, and ~3-4 masks disappear from the flow (fact 4).

title: Crowe persistent-current cells in YBCO at 77 K, no helium
idea: Revive the 1957 Crowe cell and Buck's cryotron, where a bit is a supercurrent circulating clockwise or counterclockwise in a superconducting loop, using YBCO films grown by reactive thermal co-evaporation (no argon sputtering, no KrF excimer) and cooled by liquid nitrogen made from air. A persistent current does not decay, so cells never refresh.
why: The constraint and Fact 3: liquid nitrogen replaces helium cryogenics, and loop arrays need ~4-6 masks at 0.5 um on depreciated fabs. Risks are loop inductance capping density at ~10-100 Mb/cm2 and YBCO junction reproducibility.

title: BEOL-only oxide DRAM built in packaging-class back-end fabs
idea: First principle: channels only need high-temperature processing if they are single-crystal Si; amorphous oxide channels, ALD high-k and MIM capacitors all form below 400 C. Build the whole cell array (oxide-channel gain cells plus MIM capacitors) as back-end layers on cheap logic wafers in advanced-packaging/back-end fabs, which cost about 1/3 per wafer-pass of front-end fabs.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: runs on U.S. advanced-packaging lines being built under CHIPS, with no implanters, diffusion furnaces or EUV.

title: Army-arsenal GOCO model for a strategic U.S. DRAM fab
idea: Like the Lake City Army Ammunition Plant, the government owns the fab building and tool set and a commercial memory maker operates it under a cost-plus-fee contract, selling output commercially with a guaranteed defense allocation.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. share (1-2%): removes the private-capital hurdle and cycle risk for the first domestic high-volume fab; public cost of capital ~4% versus ~10% private.

title: MEMS micro-drum with a thousand heads and unpatterned media
idea: Revive the 1950s magnetic drum as a 2 mm MEMS rotor on an electrostatic or gas bearing spinning at ~1M rpm, coated with continuous perpendicular magnetic media and served by 1,000 fixed thin-film heads around its rim, so a wanted bit arrives within ~60 ns. Bits are defined by head field, so the media needs no lithography at all.
why: Capital and litho (Fact 4): heads come from mature HDD-head wafer fabs (~100 nm rules) and the rotor from 1 um MEMS lines; at ~1 Tb/in2 media density a 3 mm2 face holds ~5 Gb; risks are bearing wear, shock and rotational latency.

title: NAND-grade LDPC replaces DRAM redundancy, fuses and laser repair
idea: Combine NAND flash's quasi-cyclic LDPC engine with DRAM. A rate-0.85 code in the base/buffer die absorbs a 1% raw cell BER, with a ~10 ns fast path for clean lines, so the DRAM die ships with no spare rows or columns, no fuse bank, no laser-repair pass and no repair-analysis test step.
why: Redundancy and fuses take ~5-8% of die area, and laser repair plus repair test take ~5% of back-end capex; together ~10% lower cost/bit (facts 4, 7).

title: Million-tip field-emitter array writes periphery maskless in proximity mode
idea: Effect: Fowler-Nordheim tunneling. A wafer-scale array of gated Si or CNT tips, each with its own CMOS driver, flies 2-5 um above the resist; each tip writes only its own 50 um patch, so no electron column is needed, and sub-1 kV electrons keep proximity blur low. A digital data path replaces the periphery mask set.
why: Removes the $10-20M mask set per node and the EUV need for periphery layers (periphery ~49% of die, fact 7); makes design spins and low-volume U.S. production cheap.

title: Freeze the lithography roadmap; scale only by vertical tiers
idea: Worse: retire scanners at every node and buy new ones. Flip: commit to a 10-year litho-frozen DRAM roadmap at a fixed F~16-18 nm, with all density gains from deposition/etch tier stacking, so the scanner fleet fully depreciates and serves 3-4 generations.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): litho is ~25-35% of tool spend, and fully depreciated scanners cut wafer cost ~15-20%. Dep/etch tools are multi-sourced and largely U.S.-made.

title: Merchant EUV template wafers sold to DUV-only memory fabs
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action resolves 'need EUV pitch but cannot afford EUV': a central hub pre-patterns the three densest periodic layers (active islands, buried wordlines, capacitor-hole hardmask) into a durable SiN/carbon hardmask stack on blank wafers and ships them to small fabs that finish every coarse layer on DUV, aligning to marks embedded in the template.
why: Each small fab avoids $200M+ per EUV scanner and most of the 5-7 EUV layers; the hub runs scanners at >90% utilization across customers, letting several U.S. memory fabs start at ~1/3 the capex (fact 4).

title: Modules test and burn themselves in during shipping
idea: Po: the test floor is the delivery truck. Each module gets an on-board BIST controller plus small heater and supercapacitor so burn-in, march tests and retention profiling run in transit and at first boot, reporting back to the vendor; final tester insertions shrink to a quick screen.
why: Backend capital: testers and burn-in ovens are a major backend capex and capacity bottleneck; ~50% fewer tester hours per GB.

title: Defect-tolerant arrays delete half the in-line inspection tools
idea: First principle: yield is exp(-D0*Acrit), so 12% spare rows/columns plus per-subarray remap tables make yield insensitive to random defects up to ~5x today's D0. Spend that margin by skipping ~50% of optical and e-beam inspection and metrology steps (sample 1 wafer per lot) and relaxing some cleanroom zones from ISO 3 to ISO 5.
why: Capital and throughput: inspection/metrology is ~10-15% of fab tool capex and adds cycle time; ~8% capital saving for ~3% die-area overhead.

title: Grow pillars, don't dig holes: bottom-up electrode forest
idea: Reverse subtractive to additive: instead of etching high-AR holes in an oxide mold, grow conductive pillars upward from the landing pads by selective epitaxy of degenerately doped Si or SiGe, then coat them conformally with ALD dielectric and top plate.
why: Removes the hardest etch step and mold/support deposition (~10-15 steps); AR set by growth time not plasma physics, cutting etch-tool capex ~20-30% for the capacitor module.

title: Substitute shared row activation with dual-gate coincident-select vertical cells
idea: Give each vertical-channel access transistor two independent gates, the wordline on one face and a column-select line on the other, created by splitting the gate-all-around ring with one self-aligned spacer cut; a cell opens only where both lines are high, so only the requested 64-512 bits are sensed instead of an 8 KB row.
why: Constraint and fact 8: removes ~16-128x overfetch for ~10-30x lower energy per useful bit; facet: the added select needs no new lithography layer because the split is self-aligned.

title: Squeeze casting: high-pressure forced aluminum fill replacing tungsten plugs
idea: Die casting pushes molten metal into fine cavities with pressure; replace CVD tungsten contacts and landing pads with PVD aluminum forced into TiN-lined openings by a 60-100 MPa argon anneal at 400-450 C, run in batch hot-isostatic-press chambers adapted from aerospace castings.
why: W-free metallization (constraint) and RC: removes WF6 CVD and W targets; Al ~3 uOhm-cm versus 10-20 for narrow W lowers contact resistance and allows smaller contacts; batch HIP is cheap per wafer.

title: Fat landing pads printed by immersion, bridged pairs tolerated
idea: Combine enlarged storage-node landing pads with bridge-aware interleaving: overlay can drift +/-4 nm instead of +/-2 nm, and the ~1% of pads that short to a neighbor create paired errors that the code interleave is built to absorb. A 193i scanner can then replace EUV on that layer.
why: Overlay, not resolution, drives EUV on the landing-pad layer. Moving one EUV layer to immersion saves ~$100-150 per wafer and scarce EUV hours (fact 4).

title: Array buried-channel transistor reused as the only periphery transistor
idea: Combine the array's recessed-channel buried-wordline transistor with periphery logic: decoders, sense control and I/O are built only from the same BCAT-style devices (upsized, paralleled, dynamic logic styles), and the separate HKMG planar periphery module is deleted.
why: The HKMG periphery module adds ~8-12 masks plus integration complexity. Deleting it removes ~10-15% of mask count and periphery-specific tools, and more bank parallelism absorbs the speed cost.

title: Superlattice edge stamps print 16 nm wordlines without optics
idea: Constraint: pitch must come from deposition thickness, never from light. Grow a Si/SiGe superlattice of 8 nm layers, cleave and selectively recess its edge into a ridge master, metallize the ridge tips and transfer them as wordline/bitline gratings (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer), each master printing thousands of wafers through daughter stamps.
why: Fact 4: sub-20 nm pitch set by epitaxy with zero scanner time; critical-layer litho capital -50-80%.

title: Miura-fold origami: one patterned membrane folded into 16 tiers
idea: Borrowed from origami solar arrays and Miura-fold maps: pattern 16 DRAM array tiles side by side in one planar pass on a 100 nm Si/oxide membrane with thin polymer hinge lines, release it, and fold it accordion-style onto a periphery die, with interconnect running across the hinges.
why: Fact 2: turns a 16-tier 3D process into one planar 2D process, ~16x fewer critical litho passes per bit; hinge wiring and stack flatness are speculative.

title: Memory by the square meter in idle display-panel fabs
idea: Po: RAM is made in TV factories. Idle Gen-6/8.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines already run IGZO transistors; pattern 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays at ~1-1.5 um rules on glass (a ~5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 panel holds on the order of 20 GB), dice into tiles and bond them to 28 nm controller dies.
why: Capital intensity and non-EUV supply: zero new fab, no EUV, no quartz crucibles; ~$10-20/GB slower capacity tier from idle capacity, with IGZO's low leakage cutting refresh.

title: Substitute periphery photomasks with maskless digital-micromirror lithography
idea: Pattern non-critical periphery layers (thick metal, implant blocks, pads, fuses) with a DMD-based maskless DUV writer, so each layer is a data file rather than a reticle; reticles are reserved for the critical array layers.
why: Fixed cost and lead time: saves ~15-20 masks per product revision, enables fast custom HBM base-die and SKU spins, and reduces reticle-shop dependency.

title: Robotic second-life harvest of retired DRAM into CXL memory shelves
idea: DRAM reclaim from retired servers and phones has failed on manual handling, mixed generations and test cost. Decommissioning lines at hyperscalers use robots to pull DIMMs and reflow-desolder LPDDR packages, run a 10-minute BIST sort, and mount mixed DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR parts behind CXL controllers that hide generation differences in pooled second-life shelves.
why: Meets 100x: the bits are already paid for; harvest plus test ~$0.05-0.1/GB vs ~$5-10/GB new, with zero fab capex. Trades: older speeds, higher power per bit, supply tied to retirement cycles.

title: Masks grown from wafers: electroformed nickel imprint stamps
idea: Po: the mask is the product. Pattern one perfect array-layer wafer once (EUV or e-beam), electroform nickel replicas of its etched topography, and use the Ni shims (thousands per master, like CD stampers) as nanoimprint templates for the periodic capacitor and bitline layers on production wafers.
why: Litho capex and EUV dependence (fact 4): replaces 2-3 EUV array exposures with NIL at ~1/5-1/10 the tool cost; templates become cheap consumables; ~15-25% wafer-cost cut if imprint defectivity is controlled.
